title: Redis Streams & Pub/Sub: A Field Handbook
summary: A ten-chapter study-notes handbook on Redis messaging: how Pub/Sub fire-and-forget delivery differs from the persistent Streams log, how consumer groups distribute work with XREADGROUP, XACK, and the Pending Entries List, and how to recover stuck messages with XAUTOCLAIM, trim safely, and avoid the classic delivery-loss traps.

chapters.title: Two Messaging Models in One Server
points: Redis ships two independent messaging systems: Pub/Sub (since 2.0) and Streams (since 5.0) — they share no keyspace and no commands
Pub/Sub channel names are NOT keys: they live in a separate namespace, never appear in KEYS/SCAN, and are not persisted by RDB or AOF
A stream IS a key: it shows up in SCAN, has a TTL, is dumped to RDB, replayed from AOF, and replicated as normal key data
Pub/Sub semantics: at-most-once, fire-and-forget — the server pushes to whoever is connected right now and forgets immediately
Streams semantics: at-least-once with explicit acknowledgement — the entry stays in the log until you trim it, and stays in the PEL until you XACK it
Pub/Sub has zero history: a subscriber joining at t+1 can never see a message published at t
Streams are an append-only log with random access: XRANGE any past window, and many independent consumers can replay the same entries
Message retention: Pub/Sub retains nothing (O(1) memory per message, freed at once); Streams retain everything until MAXLEN/MINID trimming or key deletion
Fan-out: Pub/Sub always broadcasts to every subscriber; Streams can broadcast (independent XREAD readers) OR load-balance (one consumer group)
Comparison row — ordering: both preserve per-publisher order; Streams additionally give a globally sortable ID per entry
Comparison row — backpressure: a slow Pub/Sub subscriber gets its output buffer filled and is disconnected; a slow Stream consumer just falls behind on its own cursor
Rule of thumb: Pub/Sub for ephemeral live signals (cache invalidation, presence, live tickers); Streams for work that must not be lost (jobs, events, orders)
Redis Streams borrows heavily from Kafka's log model but is a single-key, in-memory structure — no partitions, no per-topic disk segments
Neither model is a full broker: no routing keys, no exchanges, no dead-letter queue built in — you build DLQ behavior yourself

chapters.title: Pub/Sub Mechanics: SUBSCRIBE, PUBLISH, Patterns
points: `PUBLISH channel message` returns the number of clients that received it — count is receivers, not deliveries confirmed, and excludes shard-channel receivers
`SUBSCRIBE ch1 ch2` puts the connection into subscriber mode; in RESP2 only SUBSCRIBE/UNSUBSCRIBE/PSUBSCRIBE/PUNSUBSCRIBE/PING/QUIT/RESET are legal after that
RESP3 lifts that restriction: a RESP3 client can subscribe and still run normal commands on the same connection, because push messages are a distinct protocol type
Push message shape: 3-element array `["message", channel, payload]`; pattern deliveries are 4 elements `["pmessage", pattern, channel, payload]`
`PSUBSCRIBE news.*` matches with glob-style patterns (`*`, `?`, `[abc]`) — a client subscribed both directly and by pattern gets the message twice
Pattern matching cost: PUBLISH is O(N+M) where N = channel subscribers and M = total registered patterns — heavy pattern use makes every publish slower
Introspection: `PUBSUB CHANNELS [pattern]`, `PUBSUB NUMSUB ch...`, `PUBSUB NUMPAT`, `PUBSUB SHARDCHANNELS`, `PUBSUB SHARDNUMSUB`
Keyspace notifications ride on Pub/Sub: enable with `CONFIG SET notify-keyspace-events KEA`, then subscribe to `__keyspace@0__:mykey` or `__keyevent@0__:expired`
Expired-key notifications fire when the key is actually deleted (lazy access or the active-expire cycle), not at the exact TTL instant — the delay can be seconds
Code example — cache invalidation: `PUBLISH cache:invalidate user:42` on write; every app node drops its local copy on receipt
Client-side caching (RESP3 tracking) uses the invalidation push channel `__redis__:invalidate` — same delivery mechanism, same at-most-once caveat
Subscriber output buffer limits: `client-output-buffer-limit pubsub 32mb 8mb 60` — exceed it and Redis kills the connection, silently losing everything queued
A dropped and reconnected subscriber must re-issue SUBSCRIBE; client libraries that auto-resubscribe still lose every message published during the gap
MULTI/EXEC does not make PUBLISH transactional for the receiver: subscribers see the messages after EXEC, but no subscriber ever confirms receipt

chapters.title: When Pub/Sub Loses Messages
points: Loss cause #1 — no subscriber online: PUBLISH with zero receivers returns 0 and the message is gone; there is no queue behind it
Loss cause #2 — subscriber restart or deploy: the whole redeploy window is a black hole, and nothing tells you how many messages fell in it
Loss cause #3 — slow consumer eviction: the pubsub output buffer hard limit (32mb) or soft limit (8mb for 60s) kills the client mid-stream
Loss cause #4 — network partition: TCP takes seconds to notice; messages published into a half-open socket vanish without an error to the publisher
Loss cause #5 — failover: replicas propagate Pub/Sub, but messages in flight during a primary promotion are dropped, and the client must reconnect anyway
Loss cause #6 — client-side processing crash: the message was delivered and read off the socket, then the process died before doing the work; Redis considers it delivered
Pub/Sub messages are NOT persisted: AOF and RDB never record them, so a full restart replays keys but replays no messages
Pub/Sub in Cluster: plain PUBLISH is broadcast to every node in the cluster bus — correct, but O(nodes) traffic and a known scaling bottleneck
SPUBLISH/SSUBSCRIBE (sharded Pub/Sub, 7.0) confine a channel to one slot's shard, removing the cluster-wide broadcast at the cost of slot-aware clients
The `PUBLISH` return value is the only feedback you get, and it is a liar for reliability purposes: it counts clients that had the message written to their buffer, not clients that processed it
Anti-pattern: using Pub/Sub for job dispatch — two workers subscribed to the same channel BOTH run the job (broadcast, not load-balanced)
Anti-pattern: Pub/Sub as the sole cache-invalidation transport with no TTL fallback; one missed message means a permanently stale cache entry
Mitigation pattern: treat Pub/Sub as a hint, not a source of truth — pair it with a short TTL, a version counter, or a periodic reconcile sweep
Migration signal: the moment you need 'did anyone actually handle this?', you need Streams — no amount of Pub/Sub tuning gets you delivery guarantees

chapters.title: Streams: The Append-Only Log
points: `XADD key * field value [field value ...]` appends an entry; `*` asks the server to generate the ID
Entry ID format `<ms>-<seq>`: milliseconds since epoch plus a 64-bit sequence counter for entries within the same millisecond
IDs are strictly monotonic per stream; XADD with an explicit ID smaller than the current max returns `ERR The ID specified in XADD is equal or smaller than the target stream top item`
Partial ID `XADD key 1526919030474-*` pins the ms part and lets Redis pick the sequence — useful for deterministic time bucketing
An entry is a flat field-value map, like a small hash; there is no nesting, so serialize structured payloads to JSON or MessagePack in one field
`XLEN key` is O(1); `XRANGE key start end [COUNT n]` walks the log, `XREVRANGE key end start` walks it backward (note the reversed argument order)
Range shorthands: `-` = smallest ID, `+` = largest ID; exclusive ranges use a `(` prefix, e.g. `XRANGE s (1526919030474-0 +` for cursor pagination
`XREAD COUNT 10 STREAMS mystream 0` reads from the beginning; `$` means 'only entries arriving after this call'
`XREAD BLOCK 5000 STREAMS mystream $` blocks the client up to 5s for new entries; `BLOCK 0` blocks forever
XREAD is fan-out: every reader tracks its own last-seen ID client-side, so N readers all see all entries and nothing is acknowledged
Internal structure: a radix tree (rax) of macro-nodes, each holding many entries with a shared field-name master entry — this is why streams are memory-efficient at scale
Because of delta-compressed listpack nodes, adding entries with identical field names is dramatically cheaper than varying them per entry
`XDEL key id` removes an entry but does NOT reclaim memory immediately — it just flags the entry in its macro-node; the node frees when all its entries are deleted
`XINFO STREAM key` shows length, radix tree keys/nodes, last-generated-id, max-deleted-entry-id, entries-added, first-entry and last-entry
`XSETID key id [ENTRIESADDED n] [MAXDELETEDID id]` forcibly rewrites the cursor — needed when rebuilding a stream from a backup

chapters.title: Consumer Groups: XGROUP and XREADGROUP
points: A consumer group is a named cursor plus a delivery ledger: one shared last-delivered-id, and per-consumer sets of unacknowledged entries
`XGROUP CREATE mystream mygroup $` starts the group at the tail (only new entries); `0` starts it at the head (replay everything)
`XGROUP CREATE ... MKSTREAM` creates the stream key if it does not exist — without it you get `ERR The XGROUP subcommand requires the key to exist`
`XREADGROUP GROUP mygroup consumer-1 COUNT 10 STREAMS mystream >` — the `>` means 'entries never delivered to any consumer in this group'
Any ID other than `>` (typically `0`) reads that consumer's OWN pending entries instead, returning already-delivered-but-unacked messages for recovery
Consumers are created implicitly on first XREADGROUP; no registration step, and a typo'd consumer name silently creates a new consumer that owns nothing
Load balancing: within a group each entry goes to exactly one consumer; across groups every group independently sees every entry
`XREADGROUP ... NOACK` skips PEL insertion — at-most-once delivery with the ergonomics of a group; use only when losing a message is acceptable
`XGROUP CREATECONSUMER`/`DELCONSUMER` manage consumers explicitly; DELCONSUMER returns how many pending entries were destroyed with it
`XGROUP SETID mystream mygroup 0` rewinds the group cursor to reprocess history — it does NOT clear the PEL, so old pending entries remain
`XGROUP DESTROY mystream mygroup` deletes the group and every PEL in it; entries stay in the stream, so another group can still read them
`XINFO GROUPS mystream` reports per-group name, consumers, pending count, last-delivered-id, entries-read and lag
`lag` = entries added to the stream that the group has not yet delivered; it goes NULL when the log has been trimmed past what the group tracked
Naming discipline: derive the consumer name from a stable identity (pod name, worker index), not a random UUID per process start, or restarts orphan PEL entries
Code example — worker loop: XREADGROUP with `>` and BLOCK 2000, process, XACK on success, and on startup first drain your own `0` backlog

chapters.title: Acknowledgement and the Pending Entries List
points: The PEL is a per-group table of entries delivered but not yet acknowledged, keyed by entry ID, with an owner consumer, delivery time, and delivery counter
An entry enters the PEL the instant XREADGROUP returns it — before your code has even seen the bytes on the wire
`XACK mystream mygroup id [id ...]` removes entries from the PEL and returns how many were actually removed (0 means already acked or never pending)
Acking an unknown or already-acked ID is not an error — XACK is idempotent, which makes retry-safe cleanup easy
Delivery guarantee is at-least-once: a crash after processing but before XACK means the entry gets redelivered, so handlers must be idempotent
There is no exactly-once: to approximate it, store a processed-ID set (or a unique constraint in your database) and skip duplicates on redelivery
`XPENDING mystream mygroup` (summary form) returns total pending, min ID, max ID, and a per-consumer count — cheap, safe to poll for monitoring
`XPENDING mystream mygroup - + 10` (extended form) returns per-entry ID, owner, idle milliseconds, and delivery count
`XPENDING ... IDLE 60000 - + 100 consumer-1` filters by minimum idle time and by owning consumer — the standard way to find stuck work
Delivery counter increments on every claim/redelivery; a count above a threshold (say 5) marks a poison message that should go to a dead-letter stream
PEL memory is real: an unacked backlog of millions of entries costs memory even if the stream itself is trimmed, and trimming does NOT remove PEL references
A trimmed-away entry that is still in the PEL becomes a phantom: XCLAIM/XAUTOCLAIM returns the ID with a nil entry body
Redis 7.0 fixed the cleanup path — XAUTOCLAIM deletes those phantom IDs from the PEL and reports them in its third reply element
Ordering caveat: the PEL means a group's processing is NOT strictly ordered — a redelivered old entry can be handled after newer ones
Diagnostic: `XINFO CONSUMERS mystream mygroup` shows each consumer's pending count, idle time, and (7.2+) inactive time since its last successful read

chapters.title: Recovering Stuck Work: XCLAIM and XAUTOCLAIM
points: A dead consumer's pending entries are stranded — nothing in Redis reassigns them automatically, so recovery is an explicit application job
`XCLAIM mystream mygroup new-consumer 60000 id [id ...]` transfers ownership of listed IDs whose idle time exceeds the min-idle-time argument
min-idle-time is the safety interlock: two rescuers racing to claim the same entry, and only the first succeeds, since the claim resets idle to 0
`XCLAIM ... JUSTID` returns only IDs and does not increment the delivery counter — the cheap option for bulk ownership moves
XCLAIM options: `IDLE ms` and `TIME unix-ms` to set the new idle clock, `RETRYCOUNT n` to overwrite the counter, `FORCE` to create a PEL entry for an unpending ID
`XAUTOCLAIM mystream mygroup consumer 60000 0 COUNT 100` (6.2+) scans the PEL from a cursor and claims everything idle past the threshold in one call
XAUTOCLAIM returns three elements: the next cursor (`0-0` when the scan completes), the claimed entries with their fields, and the list of deleted phantom IDs
Loop the XAUTOCLAIM cursor until it returns `0-0` — a single call only covers COUNT entries and leaves the rest stranded
Prefer XAUTOCLAIM over XPENDING + XCLAIM: one round trip, no risk of the ID list going stale between the read and the claim
Set min-idle-time comfortably above your slowest legitimate processing time, or you will steal work from a consumer that is merely busy
Dead-letter pattern: when delivery count crosses your limit, XADD the payload to `mystream:dlq`, then XACK the original so it leaves the PEL
Run the reclaim sweep from every worker on a timer (e.g. every 30s) rather than a single leader process, so recovery has no single point of failure
`XAUTOCLAIM ... JUSTID` skips fetching bodies and skips incrementing retry counts — useful for a fast rebalance after a planned scale-down
Consumer hygiene: after a scale-down, XGROUP DELCONSUMER the retired names only AFTER their PEL has been claimed away, or you destroy the pending work

chapters.title: Trimming, Memory, and Capped Streams
points: Streams grow forever by default — an unbounded stream is the #1 cause of Redis OOM in production event pipelines
`XADD mystream MAXLEN 1000 * field value` trims to roughly 1000 entries on every append
`MAXLEN ~ 1000` (approximate, with `~`) is far cheaper: it stops at a macro-node boundary instead of splitting nodes, so it may keep a few extra entries
`LIMIT n` caps the work per trim call (`MAXLEN ~ 1000 LIMIT 100`) and is only legal with the `~` form — bounding latency spikes on a huge backlog
`MINID 1526919030474-0` trims by ID rather than count — the natural fit for time-based retention like 'keep 24 hours'
`XTRIM mystream MAXLEN ~ 1000` and `XTRIM mystream MINID ~ <id>` do the same trimming out-of-band, so publishers stay fast
`XADD ... NOMKSTREAM` refuses to create the stream if it does not exist — returns nil, useful to avoid resurrecting a deliberately deleted key
Trimming is dumb about consumers: it deletes entries no matter which groups have not read them, silently losing undelivered work
Before trimming, check `XINFO GROUPS` lag or the minimum last-delivered-id across groups, and trim only up to the slowest consumer
Memory tuning: `stream-node-max-entries` (default 100) and `stream-node-max-bytes` (default 4096) control macro-node size — bigger nodes compress better but make XDEL and approximate trims coarser
Field-name reuse matters: entries whose field names match the node's master entry store only the values, so a stable schema can halve memory
`MEMORY USAGE mystream` includes the radix tree and consumer group PELs — a small stream with a huge PEL still reports large
TTL works on the whole key: `EXPIRE mystream 86400` deletes the stream, its groups, and all PELs together — a blunt but valid retention policy
Capacity math: at 1 KB per entry and 10k entries/sec, an untrimmed stream costs ~36 GB per hour — decide retention before launch, not after the alert

chapters.title: Durability, Replication, and Cluster Behaviour
points: Streams are replicated as ordinary key writes: XADD propagates with its resolved concrete ID, never `*`, so replicas stay byte-identical
Consumer group state replicates too — XREADGROUP propagates an XCLAIM-equivalent, and XACK propagates, so a promoted replica keeps the PEL
Replication is asynchronous: a primary that acknowledges an XADD and then crashes before propagating loses that entry — `WAIT numreplicas timeout` narrows but never closes the window
AOF with `appendfsync everysec` can lose up to one second of entries on a hard kill; `appendfsync always` costs throughput for near-zero loss
RDB-only persistence loses everything since the last snapshot — never the right choice for a stream you treat as a queue
Failover truth: Streams give you at-least-once ONLY as far as your persistence and replication settings allow — the ack model does not create durability on its own
Cluster: a stream is a single key living in a single hash slot, so one stream never spans nodes and one stream's throughput is one node's throughput
To scale beyond one node, shard manually into `stream:{0}` … `stream:{15}` and hash the partition key — the hash tags pin each shard to its own slot
Multi-key commands (XREAD across several streams) require all keys in the same slot in Cluster mode, or you get `CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot`
Pub/Sub in Cluster: PUBLISH broadcasts across the cluster bus to all nodes; SPUBLISH/SSUBSCRIBE restrict traffic to the shard owning the channel's slot
`XADD` inside MULTI/EXEC or a Lua script must use an explicit ID or `*` — scripts were historically restricted from nondeterministic commands, now handled by effect replication
Blocking commands (XREAD BLOCK, XREADGROUP BLOCK) do not block the server: they park the client, so a `BLOCK 0` consumer is nearly free
A blocked client still counts against `maxclients` and holds a connection — hundreds of idle blocked consumers is fine, hundreds of thousands is not
Monitoring set: `XINFO STREAM key FULL` for a deep dump (PEL contents included), `XINFO GROUPS` lag per group, and `redis-cli --stat` for throughput

chapters.title: Patterns, Pitfalls, and Choosing Your Model
points: Decision rule: is losing this message acceptable? Yes = Pub/Sub. No = Streams with a consumer group and explicit XACK
Decision rule: must exactly one worker handle each item? Streams consumer group. Must everyone see it? Pub/Sub, or one group per consumer
Pitfall — acking before processing: XACK first means a crash loses the message; always process, then ack
Pitfall — never draining your own PEL: a restarted worker that only reads `>` leaves its old pending entries stranded forever; read `0` first
Pitfall — random consumer names: UUID-per-boot leaks a dead consumer and its PEL on every restart; use a stable name or DELCONSUMER on shutdown
Pitfall — no reclaim sweep: without a periodic XAUTOCLAIM, one crashed pod silently drops its in-flight batch
Pitfall — unbounded MAXLEN: no trim policy means an OOM outage weeks later, at the worst possible traffic peak
Pitfall — trimming past unread entries: MAXLEN does not consult consumer groups, so aggressive trims delete work nobody ran
Pitfall — non-idempotent handlers: at-least-once plus a retry equals double charges, double emails, double writes; key every side effect by entry ID
Pitfall — poison messages: an entry that always throws is redelivered forever; cap on delivery count and route to a DLQ stream
Pitfall — huge COUNT with slow work: claiming 1000 entries you cannot finish before min-idle-time causes another consumer to steal and duplicate them
Pattern — Streams as an outbox: XADD inside the same MULTI as your data write, so a published event and its state change commit together
Comparison — Streams vs LIST queue (BLPOP): lists are O(1), simpler, and pop-destructive with no ack, no history, and no fan-out; streams give replay and groups at the cost of memory and complexity
Comparison — Streams vs Kafka: Kafka wins on multi-node partitioning, disk-backed retention, and ecosystem; Redis wins on sub-millisecond latency, one-command setup, and no extra infrastructure
Closing checklist: bound the stream, ack after work, name consumers stably, drain your own PEL on boot, sweep with XAUTOCLAIM, cap retries into a DLQ, and alert on group lag and PEL size
